facts.text: On this day in 1415, the Battle of Agincourt saw ~6,000 exhausted English troops defeat a French force three times their size — a victory so lopsided it reshaped European power for a generation.
On this day in 1983, the US invaded Grenada, an island of 91,000 people, deploying over 7,000 troops — more soldiers than the island had permanent residents old enough to vote.
Manila is the world's most densely populated city proper, packing roughly 111,000 people per square kilometer — denser than any place on Earth with a population above one million.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, holding about 60% of the world's fresh surface lake water within its borders.
The city of Chongqing, China, has a larger population than Australia. Its municipality — a single administrative unit — holds over 32 million people.

On this day in 1929, 'Black Sunday' preceded Black Tuesday by 48 hours — panicked investors jammed phone lines so completely that brokers couldn't execute sell orders, accelerating the very crash they were trying to escape.
On this day in 2001, Apple launched the first iPod at $399 — more than a modern iPhone adjusted for inflation. Analysts called it overpriced. It went on to save the company.

The New York Stock Exchange was founded in 1792 under a buttonwood tree, but the famously chaotic trading floor it became known for is now largely silent — over 90% of NYSE trades are executed electronically.
Saudi Aramco's 2019 IPO raised $25.6 billion, the largest in history — yet the company sold less than 2% of itself, valuing the whole enterprise at $1.7 trillion while barely letting go of the wheel.
The U.S. penny costs about 3.7 cents to produce. The government loses money on every single one, and has for over a decade, yet continues minting roughly 4 billion annually.

On this date in 1671, Giovanni Cassini discovered Iapetus, Saturn's two-toned moon — one hemisphere is jet black, the other bone white, a contrast so stark early astronomers thought the moon only existed on one side.
Your skeleton is not the same one you had ten years ago. Bone cells replace themselves continuously; most of your skeleton is younger than a decade.
Light from the Sun takes 8 minutes to reach Earth, but the photons themselves were generated in the Sun's core up to 100,000 years ago, crawling outward before their final 8-minute sprint.
On this date in 1955, the original Disneyland castle was repainted — a footnote, but the pink hue was chosen because human eyes perceive pink as receding, making the structure look taller than it is.
A teaspoon of neutron star material weighs roughly a billion tons. Neutron stars are so dense that a sugar-cube-sized chunk would outweigh every human who has ever lived.
On this day in 1415, Henry V won Agincourt. The longbowmen who shattered French cavalry were using a weapon older than the battle by 30,000 years.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. Medieval England had tenure before Tenochtitlán had walls.
On this day in 1854, the Charge of the Light Brigade killed 110 men in 20 minutes. Tennyson published his poem about it 42 days later.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She was as ancient to Caesar as Caesar is to us.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — before anyone had laid a mile of railroad track in Africa. You could have faxed someone about the Oregon Trail.

**Sonder** (n.) — the sudden realization that every passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in *The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows*, 2012. Already outpaces many centuries-old words in daily use.
**Hiraeth** (Welsh, n.) — a longing for a home you cannot return to, or one that never existed. Untranslatable in one English word, it folds grief, nostalgia, and yearning into a single breath.
On this day in 1881, Picasso was born in Málaga — and the word **prodigy** itself descends from Latin *prodigium*, meaning omen or monster. Giftedness once carried a tinge of the unnatural.

On this day in 1415, English forces won Agincourt, cementing **chevron** in military vocabulary. The word comes from Old French for *rafter*, because the V-shape resembled a roof's peak — rank and architecture sharing a geometry.

**Mamihlapinatapai** (Yaghan, n.) — a look shared between two people who both want something but neither will initiate. From one of the world's most endangered languages, it describes something almost everyone has felt and no one has named.
On this date in 2021, Bitcoin hit $60,000 for the first time after the ProShares Bfutures ETF launched — the first US Bitcoin ETF, which tracked futures contracts, not spot BTC.

On this date in 2016, Zcash launched its genesis block. The first 20,000 blocks were a 'slow-start' phase where block rewards were fractional, preventing a mining rush from capturing nearly all early supply.
Ethereum's gas limit is not hardcoded — it's a rolling miner/validator vote. Each block can nudge it up or down by 1/1024th, making it a slow-motion consensus negotiation happening every 12 seconds.
The Bitcoin whitepaper never uses the word 'blockchain.' Satoshi wrote 'chain of blocks' — the compound noun entered the lexicon through later developer shorthand, not the founding document.
Solana's clock drifts from real time intentionally. Its proof-of-history timestamps are based on SHA-256 iteration counts, not wall clocks, so the chain's internal time and UTC diverge by design.

On this date in 2015, Microsoft's ResNet-152 surpassed human-level performance on ImageNet, hitting 3.57% top-5 error vs. humans at 5.1%. The benchmark that defined a decade of vision research was effectively retired within five years of being set.

On this date in 2022, Galactica — Meta's 120B-parameter scientific language model — was pulled from public demo after 72 hours due to confident fabrication of citations and chemistry. It remains one of the fastest public AI withdrawals on record.

GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed roughly 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — comparable to the annual consumption of 4,600 average US homes, expended in a matter of months for a single model.

AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins before most structural biology labs had a chance to validate even a handful. It compressed an estimated century of crystallography work into roughly two years of compute.

The first neural network to beat a human champion at Go, AlphaGo, used 1,202 CPUs and 176 GPUs during match play against Lee Sedol in 2016. Its successor AlphaZero trained entirely through self-play in 8 hours to surpass it.
